latest_articles.title: What Do We Mean by Transparency? Conceptualizing and Operationalizing Transparency in Communication
latest_articles.abstract: By analyzing 164 articles from communication journals published between 2002 and 2024, this scoping review systematically investigates temporal trends, conceptualizations, and operationalizations of transparency research within communication studies. The analysis identifies three primary conceptual dimensions of transparency: (1) information, encompassing both visibility and interpretation; (2) relations, functioning as an intermediary between dialogue and power; (3) values and norms, reflecting the tensions between ethical ideals and institutional constraints. Operationalization of transparency has predominantly relied on informational measures, whereas relational and value-based dimensions remain comparatively underdeveloped. Increasing attention has been directed toward subjective stakeholder perceptions, emphasizing transparency as a dynamic and context-dependent construct. Overall, the findings indicate that transparency extends beyond a stable informational attribute to incorporate relational and normative functions, while its enactment remains fluid, contextually shaped, and susceptible to unintended consequences.

latest_articles.title: Understanding Toxic Behavior in Game-Mediated Social Interaction: A Systematic Review and Future Directions
latest_articles.abstract: As multiplayer online games increasingly evolve into prominent social platforms, toxic behavior (TB), a range of negative player interactions, has attracted growing scholarly attention. However, existing research remains fragmented, lacking conceptual clarity and systematic synthesis. Thus, this study conducted a systematic review of 48 empirical studies on TB, examining its definitions, classifications and measurements, correlates, perceived consequences, and coping strategies. This study identified four main approaches to defining TB, including umbrella, subconcept, impact-based approach, and intent-based approach, highlighting form and intent as key dimensions for its classification. The occurrence of TB was related to social beliefs, technological features, game-related experiences, and individual characteristics. It was perceived to harm gaming ecosystems and players’ psychological well-being and may reinforce antisocial attitudes. To combat it, players employ a range of coping strategies, including internally oriented detachment and externally oriented interventions. Finally, this study outlines future research directions and discusses its theoretical and practical implications.
affiliations: School of Arts and Communication, Beijing Normal University, Beijing, China.

latest_articles.title: AI in Journalism Education: Curriculum Development and Implementation of Journalism in BRICS Universities
latest_articles.abstract: This study employs content analysis and semi-structured in-depth interviews to examine how journalism education across BRICS countries has responded to the rise of AI and adjusted its core paradigms. In this study, BRICS refers to the expanded BRICS grouping, comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. It combines latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling of university journalism curricula with 15 interviews of China-based journalism educators. We selected 10 representative BRICS universities with journalism and communication programs as samples, after which we compiled training frameworks, syllabi, and teaching documents for all their AI-related courses, and used the LDA model to extract core topics and to conduct manual qualitative content analysis across five dimensions: course localization, technical tools, skill guidance, teaching content, and values. The interview results provided valuable supplementary insights.

latest_articles.title: From Structural Inequalities to Labor Precarity: Adoption of Digital and AI Tools in Latin American Journalism
latest_articles.abstract: While inequalities in technological access and use have been widely documented, few studies have examined their link to labor precarity and social inequality in journalism in the Global South. This article analyzes this relationship through a multilevel study of Worlds of Journalism Study data from 4,250 journalists in 11 Latin American countries. Results show that macro-level inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, is not associated with the use of advanced digital technologies, including AI, while micro-level precarity, expressed in contractual instability and excessive workloads, is. Working conditions, rather than national disparities, are key to explaining inequalities in technology adoption.

latest_articles.title: Generative Logic and the Mediatization of Politics: Deepfake Parodies and Political Reinterpretation in China
latest_articles.abstract: This study revisits the theory of the mediatization of politics in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), questioning its applicability beyond Western democracies and proposing an extension through the concept of generative logic. Drawing on the analysis of AI-generated parodies in China’s cyberspace, it examines a distinctive mode of political communication in which foreign political figures’ faces are superimposed onto characters from Chinese historical television dramas. These satirical videos construct five patterns of analogical displacement, enabling users to reinterpret international affairs through culturally familiar frameworks. Rather than merely destabilizing truth boundaries, this content reflects a locally embedded form of AI-mediated political expression shaped by the interplay of political logic , media logic , and generative logic . We conceptualize this configuration as a multi-logic communicative structure that sustains a stable yet dynamic mode of political discourse in authoritarian contexts. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of how generative technologies reshape political engagement, symbolic meaning-making, and mediated reality across diverse political systems.

latest_articles.title: The Policy Umwelt: How AI Problem Representations Render Governance Alternatives Unthinkable
latest_articles.abstract: This paper investigates how AI narratives actively constrain the horizon of conceivable governance options. Moving beyond the established finding that narratives influence policy, we argue they fundamentally prefigure the scope of the politically thinkable by creating what we term “Policy Umwelten.” Adapting Jakob von Uexküll’s concept, a Policy Umwelt describes the perceptible and actionable landscape of interventions available within a given narrative, which systematically renders alternatives invisible. We analyze three competing narratives: Existential Risk, Accelerationism, and Critical AI. We do so through a “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” analysis of their foundational manifestos. Each constructs a distinct Umwelt: Existential Risk makes global technocratic containment imperative; Accelerationism legitimizes only deregulation and market liberation; and Critical AI centers structural reform. Despite their overt conflict, these narratives converge in constructing Policy Umwelten that render a pragmatic approach to governance difficult to perceive: one that emphasizes iterative learning from empirical feedback and institutional flexibility over grand visions or predetermined certainties. The paper concludes that the most significant constraint on AI policy is not a lack of options but a collective failure of political perception. The Policy Umwelt concept thus provides a diagnostic tool for mapping ideological deadlock and identifying pathways toward more adaptive and less deterministic technological futures.
affiliations: Department of Government and International Affairs, Lingnan University, Hong Kong SAR, China
Division of Artificial Intelligence, Lingnan University, Hong Kong SAR, China

latest_articles.title: Technology-Facilitated Sexual Violence and Abuse in Asian Societies: A Scoping Review
latest_articles.abstract: Technology-facilitated sexual violence and abuse (TFSVA) has rapidly emerged as a pervasive form of gender-based violence in Asia, yet regionally grounded syntheses remain scarce. This scoping review systematically reviewed empirical studies on TFSVA in Asian societies, focusing on how cultural contexts and platform ecosystems shape victimization, coping, and governance. Using PRISMA-ScR–consistent procedures, 22 studies published between 2021 and 2025 were identified across databases and analyzed, with all included studies focusing on adult populations. Across studies, TFSVA appears as a continuum of overlapping harms, with image-based abuse and deepfakes generating persistent, networked exposure that extends into mental health distress, social withdrawal, and offline safety risks. Coping strategies are characterized by low-visibility, individualized risk management shaped by stigma and institutional uncertainty, while culture and infrastructure jointly shape harm recognition and help-seeking. The review highlights the need for comparative, platform- and governance-focused research that integrates mental health outcomes and cultural context.
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Korea University, Seoul, Republic of Korea.

latest_articles.title: “With each one, a little of you dies” – portrayals of early pregnancy loss in films and TV-series
latest_articles.abstract: The physical experience of early involuntary pregnancy loss is often combined with strong emotions, such as grief, depression, guilt, and feelings of loneliness and isolation. Perinatal loss also occurs in fictional spaces. In this article, I will discuss the representation of pregnancy loss in fifteen anglophone TV series and films from the late 1990s until present day. The thematic analysis will shed light on the emotional, social, medical, and physical dimensions of perinatal loss. The analysis is rooted in feminist Critical Discourse Analysis paying close attention to the intersection of perinatal loss with social injustice, race, gender, and sexual orientation. The sampled on-screen depictions show pregnancy loss happens to people from varied backgrounds and the experience, although initially isolating, usually evolves into a social one, with the sufferer finding consolation through the support of others. Medical dramas are more likely to depict the physicality of the experience and rarer forms of perinatal loss. However, recurring miscarriages are overrepresented compared to real-life statistics. Ultimately, on-screen depictions often stop short of linking the personal to the societal, political, and medical, and thereby fail to escape the commonly held notion that miscarriages are somehow a personal failure.

latest_articles.title: From Alarm to Bogus: Climate Migration Discourse Across German-, Spanish-, and Dutch-Language Twitter/X (2015–2023)
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how climate migration is framed on X, drawing on an initial collection of 335,221 German-, Dutch-, and Spanish-language tweets from 2015, 2019, and 2023, of which 70,110 were retained for analysis. Using BERTopic-based thematic analysis and retweet network analysis combined with qualitative framing analysis of a subsample, we show that X reproduces established victim and threat frames from legacy media while giving visibility to a distinctive bogus frame. This frame depicts climate migration as fabricated, exaggerated, or politically manipulated by elites to harm native populations. We argue that its prominence on X stems from its role as a discursive bridge between climate denialism and digital nativism. Thematic and network analyses link this frame to polarized, anti-green, climate-skeptical, and anti-migration debates, especially in German- and Dutch-language discussions. The findings demonstrate how social media reshapes climate migration discourse by amplifying conspiratorial and nativist frames.

latest_articles.title: Thailand 5.0? Reimagining the Nation’s Digital Future With Artificial Intelligence (AI)
latest_articles.abstract: Thailand stands at a critical juncture in Southeast Asia’s digital transformation, transitioning from a mobile-first society into an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled economy. Although widespread connectivity and super app ecosystems demonstrate rapid technological adoption, research—especially in communication studies—tends to examine AI development through separate lenses of policy, innovation, and inclusion. This study addresses this gap by analyzing how alignment or misalignment among these dimensions shapes whether AI-driven transformation yields equitable outcomes or reinforces inequalities. Findings indicate that despite comprehensive national AI strategies and strong commercial adoption, gaps persist between policy ambition and implementation capacity. Dependence on foreign technological infrastructures limits sovereign AI capabilities, while digital divides produce uneven access and benefits. Authority-driven diffusion accelerates scale, but often results in compliance without meaningful capability development. The study argues that without targeted interventions in capability building, sovereign infrastructure, and culturally grounded governance, Thailand’s AI transformation risks reinforcing existing inequalities rather than promoting inclusive digital development.

latest_articles.title: Toward a Unified Conceptual Framework for Participation Research
latest_articles.abstract: Public participation has gained renewed interest amid the recent crises confronting Western democracies, yet scholarly consensus on its fundamental premises remains limited. This theoretical study reconceptualizes participation as a multidimensional communicative phenomenon by identifying its core dimensions, examining the tensions among competing theoretical traditions, and developing a unifying content-agnostic analytical framework. It contributes to participation research and communication theory in three principal ways: by mapping four paradigmatic approaches to participation; by identifying conceptual bridges that integrate these otherwise fragmented traditions; and by proposing a classificatory framework grounded in the concepts of autonomy and heteronomy. Organized around the intersecting dimensions of power asymmetries and institutionalization, the framework distinguishes four typical modes of participation and enables multidimensional comparison across diverse participatory manifestations and sociocultural settings. By moving beyond hierarchical models, disciplinary compartmentalization, and purely normative classifications, it provides a common analytical language for comparing heterogeneous participatory processes.

latest_articles.title: Understanding Internal Agenda-Building: The Role of Communication Sources and Channels in Shaping Internal Issues Salience and Employee Issue Engagement
latest_articles.abstract: This study applies agenda-building theory to the novel context of internal communication, exploring how an organization’s use of internal media, through various information sources and communication channels, strategically shapes employee agendas. Through an online survey of 996 U.S. employees, results showed that interpersonal communication channels positively influenced perceived issue salience and employee issue engagement. At the same time, print media negatively influenced issue salience. In terms of communication sources, supervisors were found to positively influence employees’ perceptions of organizational issue salience, whereas peers enhanced employee issue engagement. This study contributes to internal communication, agenda-building and employee issue engagement research by showing that peers and supervisors, as internal communicators, can strategically “build” employee agendas in ways analogous to how external media influence the public. Additionally, this study underscores the critical role of personal issue involvement in shaping employees’ internal agenda and driving their engagement with organizational issues.

latest_articles.title: The Power of Brand Modesty: The Influence of Self-Effacing Brand Messages on Branding Outcomes and Purchase Behavior
latest_articles.abstract: People use self-effacement and self-enhancement as impression management strategies to present themselves positively to others. Self-effacement involves presenting oneself modestly by de-emphasizing or diminishing virtues and accomplishments. Conversely, self-enhancement involves presenting oneself in a boastful manner by overemphasizing virtues and accomplishments. We extend this knowledge to advertising by evaluating the effects of these opposing impression management strategies in brand-related communications on branding outcomes and purchase behaviors. Across four studies, brands using self-effacing rather than self-enhancing messages elicit stronger consumer attitudes and purchasing behaviors, even in the presence of monetary tradeoffs. Perceived message–brand fit moderates these effects, such that messages aligned with the brand’s identity reduce skepticism and enhance trust. Specifically, for non-luxury brands, modest, self-effacing messages are preferred, whereas for luxury brands, boastful, self-enhancing messages align with their identity and are therefore more acceptable. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of self-effacing versus self-enhancing message types depends on brand context, with non-luxury brands benefiting more from self-effacement, whereas differences between message types are attenuated for luxury brands, allowing greater flexibility in message strategy. Finally, this research highlights skepticism and brand trust as the mechanisms underlying the effects of self-effacing and self-enhancing brand messages on branding outcomes and purchase behavior.

latest_articles.title: Attitudes Toward Energy Across European Union Member States (2006–2024)
latest_articles.abstract: Our study describes European attitudes toward energy using a harmonized dataset comprising 46 waves of the Eurobarometer (2006–2024). This tracking survey covers all European Union member states; hence, our data accumulates 1,286 individual country surveys. We focus on attitudes relevant to energy transition through three complementary lenses: energy issue salience, policy priorities, and opinions on renewable energy sources. This study documents cross-national and temporal variation in attitudes without estimating the causal effects of specific energy-related European policies or contextual events. We record a marked increase in the salience of energy during crisis periods, especially Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which rapidly elevated energy’s importance in the hierarchy of public concerns. We also show that support for renewables, in the context of energy transition, coexists with affordability and security concerns in some regions of the EU, particularly in Central-Eastern and Southern Europe. To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically harmonize such a large collection of Eurobarometer waves into a single comparable dataset, enabling long-term tracking of energy attitudes across all EU member states. In addition to the substantive results, our study also points to several difficulties the Eurobarometer project faces in providing long-term monitoring of public opinion across the highly diverse member states of the European Union.

latest_articles.title: “How can a prince become a queen?”: Gender exploration and empowerment amongst VTuber live streamers
latest_articles.abstract: “VTubers” are live streamers who use 2D or 3D digital avatars to interact with audiences in real time. In this study we investigate how VTubers construct gender representations in online spaces, showing that the creation of a VTuber’s online gender is not static, but rather a dynamic process that adapts through interactions between the avatar’s design and fictive persona, their “offline” identity, and viewer engagement. We also demonstrate that while VTubers are afforded the ability to explore fluid and non-binary gender presentations, their portrayals are often sexualised. Equally, while certain VTubers foster inclusive spaces that celebrate diverse identities, others limit explicit audience expressions of gender empowerment by enforcing chat guidelines, highlighting the complexity of this area. This study thus contributes to scholarship on identity construction in avatar-mediated spaces, offering insights into how VTubers as gender representations both reflect and redefine online gender identities, especially concerning marginalised groups within live-streaming communities.

latest_articles.title: Visual Framing and Politicization of Climate Change: The Case of Fridays for Future and Extinction Rebellion in Hungary
latest_articles.abstract: This paper addresses how the visual framing practices of the youth climate movement in Hungary challenge or reinforce post-political environmental discourse. Our analysis focuses on two social movement organizations that emerged in Hungary during the 2018–2019 global wave of climate activism: Fridays For Future Hungary (FFFH) and Extinction Rebellion Hungary (XRH), with particular attention to the forms, issue frames, and emotional frames they employ. To investigate the research question of how climate movements use visual communication to politicize climate change, we combined computational and qualitative methods and undertook a visual frame analysis of N = 789 social media images and videos, circulated by two student climate movements in Hungary. Our results show that the framing of politicizing visuals follows the organizations’ general profiles and it is frequently communicated through the posting of images and videos of demonstrations, which also explains the high proportion of motivational frames, and the frequency of simple, less controversial issue frames in the case of both organizations.

latest_articles.title: Child-To-Parent Health Misinformation Interventions Among Older Parents: A Relational Understanding of Psychological Reactance
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines older adults' psychological reactance to child-to-parent health misinformation interventions by attending to relational concerns regarding parental authority, as well as how such reactance is linked to problematic health information and family communication practices. We surveyed 428 Chinese older adults aged 60 and above. Structural equation modeling indicates that threat to behavioral freedom and threat to parental authority function as factors of reactance, with threat to parental authority conceptualized as a role-based social value threat. Psychological reactance is associated with orientations toward older adults' practices often discussed as problematic in health and family communication contexts, including tendencies toward unverified health information sharing and avoidance of health-related communication with adult children. Perceived communication style was central: autonomy-supportive prevention was negatively associated with both threats, whereas controlling prevention was positively associated with both. Correction was mainly associated with threat to behavioral freedom, although autonomy-supportive correction was directly associated with lower health communication avoidance. These results advance theoretical understanding of psychological reactance as a relationally embedded phenomenon and offer insights into factors associated with problematic health information practices and intergenerational communication among older adults.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin
University of Connecticut, Michigan State University

latest_articles.title: Memorable Health Messages on Social Media

We employ thematic co-occurrence analysis to examine co-occurrences among types of memorable messages and health beliefs and behaviors (RQ3). We denoted two co-occurrence relationships, one relationship ("A") between universalized health prescriptions and verifying the information and/or making lifestyle changes, and one relationship ("B") between individualized health encouragement and enhancing health autonomy. An overwhelming majority of memorable messages reported were from creators or influencers that participants did not follow or interact with beforehand, complicating the longstanding assumption that memorable messages emerge primarily from interpersonal relationships. We extend ToMM by conceptualizing memorable messages as platform-mediated communicative artifacts, complicating implicit understandings of message memorability, proposing a normativity-autonomy continuum, and centering health information management practices as mechanisms that might explain how memorable messages shape health beliefs and behaviors.

latest_articles.title: Digital Footprint Capital: AI, identity, and the algorithmic governance of creative work
latest_articles.abstract: Digital footprints, once regarded as incidental traces of online interaction, have become central to the organization of creative labour. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), these traces function not only as markers of identity but as forms of symbolic, reputational, and economic capital that mediate visibility, opportunity, and legitimacy within cultural and creative industries. This article introduces the concept of Digital Footprint Capital (DFC) to theorize how creators cultivate and mobilize online presence across four analytically derived dimensions: visibility capital, authenticity capital, collaborative capital, and resilience capital. Drawing on a systematic and reflexive synthesis of scholarship on digital identity, creative labour precarity, AI and algorithmic governance, the framework demonstrates how AI simultaneously expands creative possibilities and intensifies structural vulnerabilities. While generative AI accelerates content production and cultural circulation, it also reproduces inequalities, amplifies reputational fragility, and deepens pressures on digital wellness. Through documented empirical examples from platformed creative work, the article shows how digital footprints are co-constructed by human and algorithmic actors, producing hybrid identities that are both strategic and unstable. By conceptualizing digital traces as capital, this study advances debates on the datafication of cultural work and offers a framework for anticipating the evolving dynamics of AI-mediated creative economies.

latest_articles.title: The strategic provocation of digital hate: empowered targets’ perceptions of perpetrators and bystanders
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates how scholars, as empowered individuals who have been personally targeted by digital hate, perceive perpetrators and bystanders, with an emphasis on power imbalances. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 24 university professors from Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden, it reveals that scholars perceive digital hate not only as driven by ordinary citizens, but also as strategic provocation initiated by high-status actors, such as political parties or movements, who, while not explicitly involved in digital hate incidents, trigger broader public aggression. In terms of bystanders, their interventions were often perceived as insufficient due to fear, lack of expertise, or power asymmetries. Notably, scholars emphasized that while individual support provided emotional relief, effective intervention requires either intervention by empowered individuals or coordinated collective responses. The findings highlight the limitations of individual responses and underscore the need to reframe bystander intervention strategies when addressing digital hate against societally empowered individuals.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: I Know How You Feel About Me Now: A Longitudinal Investigation of the Accuracy of Meta-Liking Judgments
latest_articles.abstract: Being liked and feeling included in social groups is important for one’s well-being and self-esteem. In addition, an accurate perception of one’s social relationship is a prerequisite for successfully managing social situations, especially in phases of social reorientation such as the first semester of university. The present, pre-registered research studies the longitudinal development of meta-liking accuracy and reciprocity in two cohorts of psychology freshmen ( N = 52 and N = 70) during the first semester of university. Our results indicate that students knew who specifically liked them and that this ability slightly increased from the first week to the end of the first semester. Furthermore, students expected to be and were indeed liked back when liking specific others. These findings provide an initial insight into the role of reciprocity for meta-liking accuracy and provide starting points for future research.
affiliations: Department of Psychology, University of Münster

latest_articles.title: Obsession in Love: A Psychobiographical Study of Gwen John’s Passion for Auguste Rodin
latest_articles.abstract: Gwen John (1876–1939) is now widely considered one of the best Welsh artists, though in her lifetime she lived largely in the shadow of two flamboyant and highly successful male artists – her younger brother Augustus John and her older lover, the world-renowned sculptor, Auguste Rodin. The focus of this article is her obsessive, often tumultuous affair with Rodin which began when she was 28 and he was 64. The method used in the research is psychobiography, using psychological theory to probe behind the facts of her life as an artist in order to understand what sort of person she was and what motives and values lay behind the life choices she made. The article sets out the impact on Gwen of the loss of her mother when Gwen was eight, and her struggles to find an emotional equilibrium while at the Slade School of Fine Art. The main psychological theory used in the analysis is limerence, a comparatively new term which describes a state of manic love or total obsession with one’s lover. Her love affair with Rodin is set out in accordance with the five stages of limerence, which I call readiness, epiphany, addiction, dissipation and rebuilding. The study opens up a number of questions about obsessive love, including the dividing line between positive passion and harmful obsession and the possibility of a positive side to obsessive devotion.
affiliations: School of Business, Education and Law, University of Huddersfield

latest_articles.title: How structural and cultural violence shape journalists’ experiences and coping strategies: An intersectional analysis
latest_articles.abstract: While many studies have focused on direct and external attacks threatening journalists’ safety, this article examines how journalists experience and cope with structural and cultural violence emanating from within the journalistic field itself. This study analyzes 33 in-depth interviews with a diverse sample of journalists in French-speaking Belgium – including freelancers, journalists without press cards, and minority journalists. The analysis reveals how intersecting identity markers (gender, race, age), organizational factors (employment status, beat), and newsroom culture shape journalists’ experiences of three forms of structural violence: discrimination, trauma exposure, and economic precarity. Discrimination experienced by minority journalists elicits primarily resilience strategies; trauma exposure associated with certain beats leads to emotional withdrawal and mental health conditions; while economic violence, particularly acute among freelancers, results mostly in compliance and avoidance strategies, which can result in burn-out or exit from the profession. Crucially, cultural violence emerges as normalizing these harms by dismissing microaggressions, framing trauma as inevitable, and presenting precarity as vocational sacrifice. The study reveals that journalists face these difficulties largely in isolation, with individual coping strategies proving exhausting and unsustainable over time, highlighting the need for institutional support.
affiliations: Observatory for Research on Media and Journalism (ORM), Catholic University of Louvain, Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium

latest_articles.title: The institutional logic of news source selection in clentelistic media systems: A comparative study of Albania and Kosovo
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines source diversity in broadcast news in Albania and Kosovo’s hybrid clientelist media systems. Drawing on institutional theory, we explore how sourcing practices reflect competing logics of power, professionalism, and market pressures under conditions of uncertainty. Using a mixed-method approach that combines content analysis of prime-time news with survey data from journalists, we assess both the visibility of political and societal actors and the factors shaping source selection. Findings reveal persistent elite-centric sourcing patterns, with significant variation between the two countries. Albanian journalists report stronger influence from media owners, managers, and government institutions, indicating a highly hierarchical and clientelist structure. In contrast, Kosovo’s media system exhibits a more fragmented and fluid environment. Theoretically, this research challenges assumptions that institutionalized routines uniformly produce news source homogeneity or that clientelist systems completely suppress pluralism. By situating source diversity as a proxy for power distribution, the study contributes to debates on journalism in transitional democracies and highlights the tension between normative ideals and the realities of hybrid clientelistic media systems.
affiliations: Department of Journalism and Communication, University of Tirana

latest_articles.title: Ventriloquial Moves in CEO Open Letters: Modulating Multiple Voices for the Rhetorical Construction of Commitment
latest_articles.abstract: CEO open letters are typically studied as monovocal texts whose persuasive force derives from the formal authority of CEOs. This paper challenges that premise. Drawing on Cooren’s ventriloquial theory, it characterizes these letters as polyphonic artifacts in which CEOs modulate multiple voices. Specifically, it introduces the notion of ventriloquial move (a configuration of ventriloquial effects that fulfills a unitary persuasive function within the text) to argue that the persuasive force of these letters depends neither on the CEO’s formal position nor on the accumulation of ventriloquial effects, but emerges from an architecture of ventriloquial moves that unfolds across the text. To develop and illustrate this concept, I analyze the open letters of three CEOs –Larry Fink (BlackRock), Wael Sawan (Shell), and Jamie Dimon (JPMorgan Chase)– published under a shared communicative pressure: the ESG controversy in the United States during 2022–2023.

latest_articles.title: The Great Wall of the Press: Layered Boundary Work of AI-Integrated Journalism
latest_articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in journalistic practice, debates often frame it as either a disruptive force or a tool for efficiency. This study moves beyond this dichotomy by examining how journalists themselves interpret, negotiate, and position AI within journalism. Drawing on 19 in-depth interviews with Chinese journalists, and informed by boundary work and boundary object perspectives, the study analyses how AI is selectively integrated, justified, and governed across journalistic processes. The findings show that AI is primarily confined to routine and low-risk tasks, while being excluded from core editorial functions involving judgement, meaning-making, and accountability. The study argues that AI intensifies journalistic boundary work because it challenges journalism not only operationally, but also epistemically and infrastructurally. Journalists therefore engage in layered forms of boundary negotiation that operate across task, discursive, and structural dimensions. At the same time, AI functions as a boundary object mediating relationships among journalists, technology companies, and governance institutions under conditions of asymmetric platform dependency and institutional control.

latest_articles.title: Twi-XL: An Infrastructure for Cross-Media Research in the Netherlands
latest_articles.abstract: In the domain of media and communication research, copyright and privacy issues provide significant obstacles to achieving the strategic goals of open science. Investigating the role of different media in shaping public debates is especially difficult, as research across different media collections and platforms is not yet systematically supported by open research infrastructures on a global scale. Moreover, the private ownership of crucial communication spaces such as social media results in unreliable access opportunities for researchers and unclear conditions regarding the completeness and integrity of data where platform owners provide their own archives. This also creates obstacles for users without a technical background who are interested in gathering information, exploring, or making sense of big data. In response to these challenges, a consortium of two universities (the University of Amsterdam and the University of Groningen), two national archives (the National Library of the Netherlands and the Netherlands Institute for Sound & Vision), and SURF as a national research IT supporter created Twi-XL: Designed to facilitate cross-media research, it provides a research environment in which users of varying computational skill levels can apply automated methods to a range of archival collections, including websites, public broadcasts, radio and podcast transcripts, and over 10 years of Dutch tweets. The societal relevance of Twi-XL lies in creating a user-friendly tool that can be used by researchers to analyze societal phenomena across social media and traditional media, capturing how public debate unfolds across interconnected media environments. We describe and demonstrate the functional logic of Twi-XL with two use cases focused on: (a) social media affordances and users’ practices of news sharing, and (b) the broader public debate on sexual misconduct. Going beyond the dominance of the English language in cross-media research, our results not only showcase the advantages of developing cross-media infrastructures specific to the Dutch language, but also how Twi-XL can be utilized in qualitative and quantitative research. Embedding Twi-XL in the broader discussion on transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility, we discuss the implications and feasibility of such infrastructures, particularly for analyzing social media content.

latest_articles.title: Affective Legitimacy and Digital Populism: Evidence from Romania’s Annulled Presidential Elections
latest_articles.abstract: On 6 December 2024, Romania’s Constitutional Court annulled the first round of presidential elections, triggering an exceptional crisis of democratic legitimacy in post-communist Europe. While procedurally justified, the decision sparked intense public reactions, both emotional and political. The findings confirm that populist interpretations of institutional actions proliferate in fragmented and emotionalized digital media environments, where distrust is personalized and intensified. Drawing on a nationally representative survey (N = 964), conducted by IRES shortly after the annulment, the study examines how Romanian citizens perceived the legitimacy of the Court’s decision and identifies the key socio-political and media-related factors shaping these perceptions. Binary logistic regression and mediation models were used to assess the drivers of perceived illegitimacy. TikTok use, negative emotions (anger, disappointment, resentment), political distrust, and anti-establishment party support significantly increase the likelihood of viewing the decision as illegitimate, whereas trust in journalists reduces it. The study contributes to the literature on populism as a communicative style and emotional register, showing how legitimacy itself becomes a contested symbol in digital environments marked by personalization, fragmentation, and affective intensification. We argue that institutional legitimacy is no longer grounded solely in procedural legality but is increasingly shaped by emotionally resonant narratives circulating through digital platforms. We complement the survey with a headline-level media analysis (N = 3,923; Dec 2024 - Aug 2025), to serve as a contextual counterfactual: instead of escalating antagonism, mainstream media gradually stabilize institutional language. A keyness comparison shows that the Early window (first 14 days) is driven by institutional/legal terms (CCR, decision, annulment), while the Late window becomes actor-centric (Simion, Antonescu, Ponta, Bolojan). Over time, lexical entropy declines markedly, signaling a standardization of vocabulary around procedural frames rather than escalating antagonism. Taken together, the results point to a decoupling between media normalization and individual affect, suggesting that democratic legitimacy in platformized communication environments is increasingly produced through affective legitimacy rather than procedural authority.

latest_articles.title: Entertainment as Trojan Horse: Voluntary Consumption of Propaganda in China
latest_articles.abstract: For authoritarian propaganda to change hearts and minds, it must first reach the masses and capture their attention. In an era of media proliferation, what can an authoritarian regime do to make ordinary citizens consume pro-regime propaganda voluntarily? How can it lower citizens’ resistance to being indoctrinated? In this article, we answer these questions by studying a new generation of propaganda movies in contemporary China. Leveraging observational data and a pre-registered survey experiment, we find that entertainment elements in propaganda movies – both personality-based and narrative-based – play a key role in appealing to viewers and increasing consumption; this effect is especially pronounced among groups that are the least inclined to expose themselves to propaganda in the first place. Also, viewers are more receptive to political indoctrination when it is interwoven with entertainment, even when they recognize such content. Combined, these findings highlight the importance of entertainment in authoritarian propaganda: not only does it serve as a vehicle to disseminate political indoctrination, but it also functions as a source of appeal that renders such indoctrination more palatable to the masses.

latest_articles.title: At-risk subjects or casual content creators? User and expert perspectives on direct-to-consumer genetic testing and genetic identity work on YouTube
latest_articles.abstract: With a commercial testing kit, people can test for genetic diseases and predispositions at home without the assistance of medical institutions. The DIY tests have fundamentally reshaped the accessibility of genetic information. This article examines conflicting user and expert discourses on direct-to-consumer genetic testing in 27 YouTube-videos. While genetic experts are wary of the tests and tend to enforce professional gatekeeping around potentially impactful genetic information, test users utilize the tests as rich bio-narrative – rather than purely diagnostic – technologies that occasion interesting and affectively engaging acts of storytelling. These narratives can be used to gain visibility on the platform and, entangled with other forms of knowledge about the self, in performances of genetic identity work. Paradoxically, expert videos emulate a range of aesthetic and stylistic characteristics from user videos. These new hybrid forms of health communication pinpoint the challenges of performing expert identities on algorithmically curated platforms today.

latest_articles.title: Queer from the start: The utopianism of LGBTQ+ NFT collectors
latest_articles.abstract: While much has been written about the volatility of digital assets, academic scholarship has largely overlooked how blockchain technologies have been adopted and reimagined by LGBTQ+ communities. This article addresses that gap through a digital ethnography of queer NFT communities active during the crypto craze of 2022, combining online participant observation with semi-structured interviews. Drawing on José Esteban Muñoz’s concept of queer futurity, it examines how queer users imagined blockchain as a speculative platform for alternative economic and social possibility—despite the financial risks embedded in the technology’s libertarian and capitalist structures. The article interrogates the utopian rhetoric of inclusion, decentralisation, and wealth redistribution that was deployed within these communities to justify their interest in and holdings of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and cryptocurrency. Queer leaders leveraged the blockchain to foster inclusive digital communities and promote wealth circulation amongst LGBTQ+ individuals, while community members embraced the technology as a risky opportunity for queer economic mobility. The article positions blockchain as a contested site where competing futurities collide—offering the illusion of liberation and the reproduction of existing inequalities. It argues that while queer users sought to make the blockchain ‘queer from the start,’ their efforts were ultimately constrained by the capitalist logics that underpin the technology.

latest_articles.title: The strategic self: Functional differentiation of first-person singular reference in presidential nomination speeches
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how presidential candidates construct multifaceted political identity through first-person singular pronouns in U.S. nomination acceptance speeches from 1944 to 2020. Employing Systemic Functional Linguistics as the analytical framework, the research identifies six functionally distinct roles of ‘I’ through corpus analysis of 2613 instances across 38 speeches, each role characterized by specific combinations of process type and temporal orientation. These roles address three rhetorical imperatives that candidates must navigate simultaneously: establishing authority, building credibility, and articulating vision. Analysis indicates the persistence of all six roles across the 76-year period, while their distribution remains closely comparable across party lines, suggesting they reflect demands intrinsic to the acceptance speech rather than partisan preference or individual style. This study provides a replicable approach for analyzing functional differentiation in pronoun usage, connecting grammatical features with communicative functions and identity construction in political discourse.
affiliations: School of International Studies, Sun Yat-sen University, China

latest_articles.title: Asking About Violence in Antenatal Care: How Wording and Timing Shape Response Opportunities
latest_articles.abstract: Routine enquiries about violence in antenatal care are recommended in many countries, yet little is known about how such questions are designed in practice and how different ways of asking may shape pregnant women's opportunities to respond. This study examines how midwives ask about violence in Norwegian antenatal care consultations. These data comprise 35 video- and audio-recorded first and second antenatal consultations with eight midwives, of which 20 included routine enquiries about violence. Using conversation analysis, we identified four recurring question formats: bare category questions, post-answer specifications, within-question specifications and concrete-act questions. Bare category questions treated violence as a self-evident gloss and commonly occasioned minimal, sequence-closing denials. Post-answer specifications introduced clarification only after an initial denial, thereby reinforcing the answer rather than reopening the enquiry. Within-question specifications progressively unpacked the category of violence before a response was required, making narrative or transformative responses relevant next actions. Concrete-act questions avoided category labels altogether and instead invited responses to specific behaviors, supporting uptake based on lived experiences. Taken together, the findings show that routine violence enquiry cannot be understood as a uniform yes/no screening item: rather, whether, how, and when "violence" is specified or described through word selection may influence what types of responses become relevant. The study contributes to health-communication research by demonstrating how guideline-recommended questioning is accomplished turn by turn and discusses implications for communication training and policy implementation in antenatal care.

latest_articles.title: Social Media Influence on Tobacco Policy Support: The Role of Cancer Worry and Smoking Status in a Moderated Mediation Framework

We found that cancer worry mediated 4.6% of the total effect, with smoking status positively moderating this pathway. While nonsmokers showed higher baseline support, smokers exhibited steeper increases in policy backing as cancer worry intensified. Results aligned with the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) model, suggesting targeted social media messaging could enhance tobacco policy advocacy, particularly for smokers with familial cancer risks. The study offers theoretical contributions to public health and health communication, as well as practical implications for policymakers and the general public.

latest_articles.title: Bridging the Divide: Examining the Impact of Threat Perceptions on Prejudice Towards Afghan Immigrants in Iran
latest_articles.abstract: This research delved into the influence of perceived threat (realistic threat, symbolic threat, negative stereotypes) on the prejudice of Iranians towards Afghan immigrants. Data were collected from 416 Iranians over 18 years old. The findings revealed that threats, both individually and collectively, remained significant predictors of prejudice, even after accounting for the effects of intergroup contact and in-group identification. Notably, among the in-group identification modes (glorification and attachment), only glorification was significantly associated with prejudice.

latest_articles.title: Catalysts for Connection: How Cultural Distance and Social Motivations Shape Media Use and Identity for Chinese International Students
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how social motivations shape social media use and cultural identity among Chinese international students during the Spring Festival. Drawing on Uses and Gratifications theory and acculturation research, we test a conditional process model linking family reunion and community belonging motivations to cultural identity through informational and entertainment-oriented social media use, with objective cultural distance moderating motivation–use associations. Results reveal significant mediation and selective moderation: associations were stronger in low-distance Asian contexts for family reunion motivation–entertainment use and community belonging motivation–informational use. The findings show how culturally proximate environments intensify connection-oriented social media engagement during culturally salient moments.

latest_articles.title: A scoping review of anglophone scholarship on trauma and journalism in sub-Saharan Africa
latest_articles.abstract: This scoping review maps anglophone scholarship on trauma and journalism in and/or about sub-Saharan Africa published between 1990 and 2025. Rather than assuming a single universal definition of trauma, the review examines how trauma is implicitly and explicitly conceptualised within this literature. Drawing on 139 peer-reviewed journal articles identified through searches of four academic databases, the review analyses patterns in trauma type, methodology, country focus, authorship location, and media platform. The findings indicate that trauma is conceptualised inconsistently across the literature, with only 28% of studies explicitly employing the term. Trauma coverage nevertheless closely mirrors regional crisis contexts. Conflict and war dominate studies focused on Nigeria, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Somalia, while political and societal trauma cluster around election-related violence in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. Violence and crime, particularly gender-based violence, are most prominent in South African scholarship. Since 2010, journalist safety has emerged as a growing area of concern, particularly in Zimbabwe, Nigeria, and South Africa, while health-related trauma remains comparatively marginal despite the continent’s significant disease burden. Qualitative methods dominate the reviewed literature, while quantitative and mixed-methods research remain limited. Patterns of authorship further suggest differences in knowledge production in which Africa-based scholars more frequently produce locally grounded qualitative research, while non-Africa-based scholars disproportionately publish conceptual or theoretical work. The review identifies important conceptual, geographic, and methodological gaps and argues for more contextually grounded and trauma-informed approaches to journalism research relating to sub-Saharan Africa.
affiliations: and the Dart Center for Journalism and Trauma Research Laboratory, The University of Tulsa

latest_articles.title: China’s mediated public diplomacy on climate change: Cross-media dynamics between Chinese, US, and UK news outlets
latest_articles.abstract: This research investigates China’s mediated public diplomacy on climate change in the context of China’s “Media Going Global” campaign and its pursuit for leadership in global climate governance. Utilizing mixed computational analyses on a 6-year news corpus (2020-2025), this study examines the potential of China’s outward news channels shaping the salience of China-related climate issues in American and British media. It finds that, while China succeeds in ensuring its climate commitments acknowledged in foreign coverage, foreign evaluations of its climate actions remain largely independent of its mediated messaging. This article underscores the significance of considering the nature of issue when examining mediated public diplomacy. Climate change, unlike more contentious political issues, enables some alignments between China and western media through shared acknowledgment of climate crisis and China’s pivotal role, but remains limited to swing China’s climate image.

latest_articles.title: Conflicts of Interest Between Systemic and Corruptive: A Conceptual Compass for Watchdog Science Journalists
latest_articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism is essential to scrutinise the structural and financial conditions of scientific research. As a crucial part of this system, experts play a pivotal role in shaping knowledge, guiding policy, and influencing societal decisions. Their credibility is embedded in a complex web of relationships that brings about different conflicts of interest (COIs). Yet, journalists’ ability to uncover entanglements and ensure accountability is limited by often incomplete disclosure and conceptual vagueness of what exactly constitutes a COI. Using (bio-)medical research as an example, we develop a multidimensional typology of COIs, based on an extensive review of academic literature and disclosure frameworks in science, practice, and policy-making. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive mapping of structural, social, and material factors in a single overview to date. While not all these interdependencies are inherently problematic for a functioning research system, they still require journalists to navigate them and carefully evaluate their significance. To facilitate this, the framework also serves as both a matrix and a corrective for potential AI-based systems detecting COIs. Even though transparency and critique are central to watchdog science journalism, journalists should also be careful not to undermine public trust in science generally. Conflicts have to be evaluated carefully but without portraying science funding as inherently corrupt—thus feeding narratives of science-related populism. By foregrounding the systemic nature of COIs, this perspective supports reflection on professional norms, strategies, and principled decision-making in investigative reporting—also regarding journalism’s own entanglements with individual and third-party interests.

latest_articles.title: Political Scandals in Germany (2001–2023): A Systematic Approach to Building a Public Dataset
latest_articles.abstract: Political scandals are recurrent across democratic systems, yet research often focuses on isolated, high-profile cases, limiting generalizability and comparability. While some studies examine broader collections of scandals to identify generalizable patterns, they rarely make underlying data publicly available—restricting opportunities for replication, validation, and comparative studies. This article addresses these limitations by introducing an open-access dataset of political scandals and scandalization attempts involving federal-level politicians in Germany between 2001 and 2023. The dataset is based on a content analysis of newspaper coverage from four national-level outlets: Die Tageszeitung , Der Spiegel , Die Zeit , and Die Welt . An initial corpus of 31,274 documents was filtered to include those in which the full names of federal politicians co-occurred with the keywords Skandal (scandal) or Affäre (affair). Manual coding identified scandal-related content and assigned it to unique cases. Documents were annotated with metadata (e.g., outlet, publication date) and contextual variables (e.g., party affiliation, government/opposition status, gender). The final dataset contains structured data derived from 3,005 articles linked to 199 scandals and scandalization attempts, with over 10 variables per observation capturing publication metadata and political context. The dataset is accessible via an online repository and a web application for filtering and visualizing scandal cases and associated media coverage. The article discusses use cases for the dataset and describes how the approach can be applied across different political and media systems to produce comparable datasets.

latest_articles.title: The Emerging Practices of Watchdog Science Journalists in Ibero-America
latest_articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism (WSJ)—investigative journalism whose objects are scientists and scientific institutions—is an important way of complying with the public service commitment of journalism. It is also one of the instruments to uphold the integrity and independence of scientific research in the face of misconduct, corporate and political interference, ideological manipulation, and scientific misinformation. But science journalists often find themselves in a “too close for comfort” relationship with scientists, which can compromise their critical stance. This problem is even harder in Ibero-America, a cultural region encompassing Spain, Portugal, and Latin American countries. Here, investigative journalism has historically been less prevalent, and science journalism consolidated later. But recent outstanding journalistic work suggests the emergence of a vibrant investigative science journalism scene in the region. In this study, we explore this development by interviewing 15 journalists from Ibero-America who have carried out outstanding WSJ on science, health, and technology. Based on their answers, we identify practices, values, impacts, barriers, and facilitators of WSJ in the region. We also identify what they perceive as constraints specific to Ibero-America, including political interference, lack of transparency, disabling newsroom culture, precarious funding, problematic relations with scientists, misuse of results, and job and psychological instability. For each of these challenges, we also identify enabling actions that are fostering or could foster WSJ in the region. Our work signals a departure from historical trends and ingrained practices, calling for a reconsideration of the contribution of Ibero-America to global science journalism.

latest_articles.title: Posting under pressure: Politicians active on social media are more stressed
latest_articles.abstract: While social media has become an indispensable tool for politicians’ communication with citizens and other stakeholders, emerging qualitative evidence suggests that its use may be associated with diminished well-being and reduced performance within the parliamentary arena – potentially undermining democratic processes. Combining insights from a representative survey study of politicians in Denmark ( n = 1233) with data on their observed social media usage (Facebook: 24,625 posts; Instagram: 13,019 posts), this study is the first to test the generalizability of this emerging evidence and advance our theoretical understanding of the conditions under which politicians’ social media usage is connected to stress. The study demonstrates a significant, positive correlation between politicians’ social media usage and self-reported stress symptoms and points to excessive usage as the primary explanation behind the association. Furthermore, exposure to online harassment is a crucial mediating factor in the association.
affiliations: Department of Political Science, Aarhus University, Denmark

latest_articles.title: Kamala is Brat: TikTok and the Affective Politics of Memes
latest_articles.abstract: In this article, we examine TikTok memes about former Vice president Kamala Harris that circulated through the digital registers of the Charli XCX-inspired “Kamala is Brat” trend. By analyzing the form, function, and affective resonance of these memes, we explore how creators interpreted and reframed Harris’s image leading up to the 2024 U.S. presidential election. Using a multimodal analysis, we introduce a three-layer analytic that distinguishes memetic form, communicative function, and affective character. Our findings show how creators mobilized recognizable meme templates, narrative positioning, and affective cues to recast Harris through identity-signaling and aesthetic contrast to her opponent. We also find that TikTok’s features enabled a pop culture intertextuality in which other viral trends – including the appeal of “it girl” Julia Fox, and the symbolic ambiguity of signifiers ranging from Pulp Fiction, The Matrix, and coconuts – become linked to the candidate. We argue that platform-native meme cultures on TikTok operate as mechanisms of vernacular electoral mediation, enabling creators to reinterpret candidate imagery and political narratives through the aesthetic conventions of platform culture. In doing so, this work demonstrates how participatory meme practices contribute to the symbolic construction of electoral candidates in contemporary digital media environments.
